title: RAF Spy Plane Narrowly Avoids Disaster in 'Most Dangerous' Russian Interception Since 2022
summary: It was a routine surveillance flight over international waters — until two Russian fighters turned it into a high-stakes game of chicken. Last month, an unarmed RAF RC-135W Rivet Joint spy plane was "repeatedly and dangerously" intercepted by a Russian Su-35 and Su-27 over the Black Sea, the UK Ministry of Defence revealed on Wednesday. The Su-35 approached so aggressively that it triggered the Rivet Joint's emergency systems, disabling its autopilot. Meanwhile, the Su-27 made six passes directly in front of the RAF aircraft, closing to a heart-stopping six metres (19 feet) from its nose. Defence Secretary John Healey condemned the "unacceptable" flybys, praising the RAF crew's "outstanding professionalism" under pressure. "This incident is another example of dangerous and unacceptable behaviour by Russian pilots, towards an unarmed aircraft operating in international airspace," Healey said. "These actions create a serious risk of accidents and potential escalation." The MoD called it the most dangerous Russian action since September 2022, when a "rogue" Russian pilot fired two missiles at a Rivet Joint over the Black Sea. One missile missed; the other malfunctioned, though Russia initially blamed a "technical malfunction." The latest incident comes amid heightened tensions. The MoD pointed to increased Russian aggression in the region, including recent submarine activity near critical underwater infrastructure in the North Sea. The Rivet Joint, operated by No 51 Squadron from RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire, uses advanced sensors to gather real-time intelligence. Its mission was a routine flight to bolster NATO's eastern flank. Healey stressed the UK would not be deterred: "This incident will not deter the UK's commitment to defend NATO, our allies and our interests from Russian aggression." But the close call raises urgent questions about the risk of miscalculation. With Russian jets buzzing unarmed NATO aircraft, the margin for error is razor-thin. As one defence analyst put it, "You don't need a missile to cause a catastrophe — at those distances, a sneeze could be deadly." For now, the RAF crew is safe, but the skies over the Black Sea remain a powder keg.
why_it_matters: This near-miss shows how easily a single aggressive move by a pilot can trigger a chain reaction that pulls NATO and Russia into a direct military confrontation, affecting global security and even the daily lives of teenagers far from the Black Sea.

background_read: The Black Sea, bordered by Ukraine, Russia, Turkey, Romania, Bulgaria and Georgia, has been a strategic flashpoint since Russia annexed Crimea in 2014. NATO routinely conducts surveillance flights there to monitor Russian military movements.

The RAF’s RC-135W Rivet Joint is a modified Boeing aircraft packed with advanced sensors that ‘listen’ to electronic signals, providing intelligence without carrying weapons. No 51 Squadron operates the fleet from RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire, England.

John Healey, the UK’s Defence Secretary (the minister responsible for the armed forces), condemned the Russian actions. Similar interceptions have happened before: in September 2022, a Russian Su-27 pilot fired two missiles at a Rivet Joint; one missed, the other malfunctioned.

NATO (the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a military alliance of 30+ countries founded in 1949) has an ‘eastern flank’ of member states near Russia. Air patrols aim to reassure those allies and deter aggression, but each close encounter carries the risk of a deadly misunderstanding.

perspectives.description: The UK government’s firm condemnation and the crew’s ‘outstanding professionalism’ demonstrate that NATO will not be intimidated. Clear, measured responses help maintain deterrence and reassure nervous eastern-flank allies that the alliance is united.

Russia’s routine use of dangerous intercepts creates a constant risk of an accidental catastrophe. Each close flyby inches closer to a mid-air collision or an overreaction that could spark a wider war, and harsh words alone may not stop the provocations.

Routine surveillance flights over international waters are legal and standard practice, but they inevitably become confrontational when rival powers test each other’s nerve. This incident fits a long pattern of Russian brinkmanship in the Black Sea since 2014.

To reduce the risk of disaster, NATO and Russia could reinforce direct communication channels between air forces — often called deconfliction lines. Future policy might also include clearer rules of engagement for unarmed surveillance aircraft operating near tense borders.
